performers: Marian Anderson, contralto; San Francisco Symphony Orchestra; Pierre Monteux, conductor
intro: Marian Anderson sings the first Kindertotenlied with Pierre Monteux and the San Francisco Symphony in 1950. Between the oboe and horn at the start and the small bells at the end, Rückert’s father watches a morning that has no knowledge of his loss.

sections.label: A · Oboe and horn before dawn
sections.mNote: The contralto joins two bare wind lines

sections.label: A′ · One father’s night
sections.mNote: Flute doubles the voice; bassoon repeats rising steps

sections.label: B · The violins reach towards light
sections.mNote: Horn and voice exchange the opening phrases

sections.label: A″ · The little lamp
sections.mNote: Oboe, flute and glockenspiel surround the last couplet

cues.title: Two winds, then Anderson
cues.text: A horn moves slowly beneath the oboe’s questioning little steps. Anderson joins them with the sun’s return: “Nun will die Sonn’ so hell aufgeh’n” — now the sun will rise so brightly. The first page has almost nothing between the contralto and these two wind instruments.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, p. 3; Rückert’s opening line, our translation. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The sun belongs to everyone
cues.text: The second couplet sets the father’s “mir allein” — me alone — against a sun that shines on everyone. Mahler brings the opening back with a flute beside Anderson’s line and the bassoon below. The melody now puts its stress on the bereaved person.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 6–8; Rückert’s second couplet, our translation. Woltjer explains the changed vocal rhythm and flute doubling: https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The horn remembers
cues.text: The horn carries the melody the voice sang earlier. Anderson has a new line against it, and the oboe presses upwards. At “ew’ge Licht” — eternal light — Mahler lets the phrase spread through the violins and outlast the sung words.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 9–14, third couplet; our translation. Woltjer discusses the horn’s vocal theme and the instrumental continuation: https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A lamp in the tent
cues.text: The last couplet brings the loss down to the size of a lamp: “Ein Lämplein verlosch in meinem Zelt” — a little lamp went out in my tent. The opening melody returns, with oboe and flute close around the contralto.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 14–17; Rückert’s final couplet, our translation. The section boundary marks the returning passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Small bells after the voice
cues.text: Anderson’s last phrase salutes the world’s joyful light. Harp and glockenspiel keep going after the voice stops. The score ends with an entire bar of silence, held under fermatas.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 17: final words, harp and glockenspiel, then a bar of rests with fermatas. The existing late cue lies within this closing passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The oboe returns over the harp
transitions.from: A · Oboe and horn before dawn
transitions.how: The oboe begins its opening phrase again while the harp rocks on D-minor notes. Glockenspiel taps continue above. The shortened introduction leads to a changed vocal rhythm, with the flute doubling Anderson and the bassoon repeating C♯–D below.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 6–8; Woltjer, song I, bars 22 onwards. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html

transitions.title: Horn and contralto exchange phrases
transitions.to: B · The violins reach towards light
transitions.how: The horn prolongs the second couplet’s closing phrase over low clarinet and bassoon. Oboe figures climb into the next passage. The horn then takes the earlier vocal tune, while the contralto answers it and the harmony moves between D minor and D major.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 9–13; Woltjer, song I, bars 36–59. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html

transitions.title: The oboe’s first phrase, softly
transitions.from: B · The violins reach towards light
transitions.how: The flute softens its running notes around the oboe’s returning melody. Horns sustain below, and the glockenspiel marks the spaces between phrases. Mahler writes zurückkehrend — returning — before the last couplet takes up the D-minor tune again.

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song I, printed pp. 3–17: oboe and horn introduction, muted strings, the violins’ rising phrases and the final harp and glockenspiel.

timeline.note: Opening duet: oboe above the first horn; the voice and strings wait.
Harp and muted violas and cellos accompany Anderson’s first stanza.
The oboe’s opening phrase returns as the father names the loss that belongs to him alone.
The first violins enter with a high melody as the voice turns towards eternal light.
Flute and oboe bring back the opening phrases before the last stanza.
Harp and strings accompany the father’s blessing of the world’s joyful light.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
